I farm only 2.6 mu, so I cannot take big risks. What I do is mostly what has worked on my own land and what I see nearby. I finished primary school, so I do not calculate too finely. I look at the field, ask around, and keep the plan steady. Wheat and maize together are the safest for me. If one side is not so good, the other still brings something. We have well water, so I will use it, but not too many times because pumping costs money. Some people in my family work outside, so labor at home is not always enough. For that reason, I keep the management simple and do the important things on time.

For wheat, I will keep the full 2.6 mu. Around early to mid October I will sow a local improved wheat seed, not the most expensive one, just the kind people around here commonly use and that comes up evenly. I will put most fertilizer before sowing, then add some urea once at jointing if the wheat color is not strong enough. I do not want to cut fertilizer too much, because if wheat turns yellow the yield drops fast. But I also cannot spend too much, so I will stay around the usual middle level. I will irrigate about three times if the year is normal: one after sowing or before winter if the soil is dry, one at jointing, one around grain filling. For maize, after wheat harvest in June I will plant quickly on the same 2.6 mu, because the turnaround is short. I will use hybrid maize seed because it yields better and most neighbors do the same. I will do shallow rotary tillage or just quick land preparation, then sow right away. Maize fertilizer will also be moderate, with part at planting and part later around the big bell stage. If rain is decent, I may irrigate once; if it is dry, maybe twice. That is my way this year: do the usual things on time, spend carefully, and avoid gambling on anything new.
